findings.claim: The catch-up goroutine calls OpenViking (ls, content/write, delete) beside the Pool workers and shares no slot with them, so up to Pool+1 requests can be in flight. Catch-up runs at start, which is when a backlog burst is drained. That breaks the plan's outcome and row r8's behavior ("never more requests in flight than the pool size"). The jobspec comment ("at most POOL_SIZE requests in flight") and the components page ("at most four OpenViking requests are in flight") now say something false. TestConsumerPoolBound never runs CatchUp, so it cannot see this.

Catch-up gets OpenViking's side from one recursive fs/ls with server defaults and ignores has_more. In the installed OpenViking source (0.5.0, server/routers/filesystem.py and fs_service.ls), recursive ls stops at node_limit=1000 and level_limit=3, and the HTTP route has no way to raise level_limit. Any file missing from a truncated listing looks absent, so every pass rewrites it, one VLM call each, every 15 minutes, forever. Its stale copy is never deleted either. Today localstack has about 235 entries and only PNGs at depth 4, so this is latent, and it was not checked against the cluster's 0.4.17. The smallest fix is to fail the pass when has_more is true. Walking folders one level at a time is the full fix.

Two events for the same key can be handled by two workers at once. Apply reads S3 before it takes the lock. If worker A reads v1, worker B then reads v2 and writes it, and A writes v1 after, OpenViking keeps v1. Catch-up compares only which files exist, so the stale content stays until the next event on that file. The delete-versus-recreate interleaving loses the file in the same way, but catch-up repairs that one. Serializing per key would close it. Any such fix must not acquire anything while it holds tree.Lock that a worker blocked on RLock already holds.
